true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Attachment size settings are no longer enforced by the upload client

The maximum is now unconditionally 10 MB, even when `type` is `attachment`. This ignores `max_attachment_size_kb` (and also caps installations configured to permit image uploads larger than 10 MB), whereas the previous code used the configured per-type limit. Users can now spend time uploading attachments that the server/site policy rejects, and sites that intentionally allow files above 10 MB cannot select them at all. Keep the configured attachment limit for attachments and use a separately defined pre-downsize input limit for images.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
API URL uploads are newly limited to 10 MB regardless of site configuration

Remote API uploads previously downloaded up to `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`; replacing that with `10.megabytes` causes a configured image limit above 10 MB to be ignored before downsizing can run. An API client supplying a URL to a valid, configured-allowed 20 MB image will now receive a failed upload/download instead of the image being processed. Use a configurable source-file ceiling that is at least compatible with the site's allowed image size (or document and expose the new API limit).

Large animated GIF uploads are converted to a single-frame image

`OptimizedImage.optimize` chooses the animated GIF path by matching the `from` path against `/\.GIF$/i`, but this call passes `tempfile.path`, whose Rack/Tempfile-generated name normally has no `.gif` extension. Consequently, even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled, an oversized GIF takes `downsize_instructions`, which uses `convert #{from}[0]` and writes only the first frame. Uploading a GIF large enough to trigger downsizing therefore silently destroys its animation; pass the original filename/format through to the optimizer or select the animated path from MIME/image metadata rather than the temporary path suffix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Updating or deleting an unknown host returns a server error

Both `update` and `destroy` use `where(...).first` and immediately call methods on the result. For an ID that does not exist, `save_host(nil)` dereferences `host.host` and `destroy` dereferences `nil.destroy`, producing a 500 instead of a not-found response. This makes stale concurrent admin edits and ordinary invalid resource requests fail as internal errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Host authorization fails for case variants of an allowed hostname

The database expression lowercases the stored host but compares it to the unnormalized `host` value from `URI#host`. URI hostnames can retain input casing, while DNS hostnames are case-insensitive. Consequently, an allowed `example.com` can reject a request whose Referer or embed URL uses `EXAMPLE.COM`, breaking embeds depending on URL casing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy host values are copied without normalization and no longer match requests

The migration inserts the old `embeddable_hosts` values verbatim using SQL, so entries such as `http://example.com` or `https://example.com/path` bypass `EmbeddableHost`'s normalization callback. Runtime lookup parses a request URL and compares only `uri.host` (for example, `example.com`) against the stored value, so these migrated hosts will never be allowed. The previous setting implementation explicitly supported scheme-prefixed values; upgrading such an installation can therefore disable all existing embeds until every host is manually edited.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration interpolates legacy host configuration directly into SQL

Each legacy host string is concatenated into an INSERT statement without quoting or parameterization. A hostname value containing a quote will break the migration, and a maliciously crafted legacy setting can alter the SQL executed during upgrade. Values should be inserted through quoted/bound SQL or normalized `EmbeddableHost` records instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when the legacy embed category setting has no database row

This dereferences `[0]['id']` from a query that returns no row when `embed_category` was never explicitly persisted or does not match a category name. A default/unused embedding configuration is a normal installation state, so the migration can abort before creating the replacement configuration. The fallback on line 14 is never reached because the exception occurs first.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.

The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
A cross-site GET can change a logged-in user's notification preference

`unsubscribe` mutates `TopicUser.notification_level` on a GET endpoint, and this action is explicitly excluded from the XHR check. Since GET requests are not protected by Rails CSRF verification, any third-party page can embed or navigate to `/t/<slug>/<id>/unsubscribe` and silently alter the notification state of a visitor who is logged into the forum. The email link needs a user-specific, unguessable unsubscribe token (or a confirmation/CSRF-protected state-changing request after the GET) rather than authorizing the change solely with the ambient session cookie.

Unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, leaving notification metadata and clients stale

The action writes and saves the TopicUser record directly instead of using `TopicUser.change`, which is the normal notification-level update path. As a result it does not set `notifications_changed_at` or `notifications_reason_id` to `user_changed`, and it does not publish the topic notification-level MessageBus event. A topic auto-watched due to a category can therefore continue to display its old automatic notification reason, and other open sessions/tabs for the user will not receive the state change.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Match counters lose updates under concurrent signup attempts

`should_block?` reads a row, increments `match_count` in memory, and saves it back. Concurrent validations can read the same count and each write the same incremented value, so some blocked-email attempts are silently omitted from the statistics. Use an atomic database update such as `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", ...)`, or lock the row, so the tracking fields remain accurate under concurrent requests.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email checks can be bypassed by changing email case

The lookup compares the submitted value directly against `blocked_emails.email` without canonicalizing it. Email local/domain case variants (for example, a block entry for `user@example.com` and a signup using `USER@example.com`) will not match on the case-sensitive database column, allowing a blocked address to register. This is especially problematic because other user-email paths use `Email.downcase`, so the application already treats emails as canonicalized for lookup purposes. Normalize both blocked-email storage and lookup (and enforce a matching normalized unique index) before querying.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Resize postMessage uses the full Referer as target origin

`request.referer` normally includes a path and query string, but `postMessage` target origin must match the embedding window's origin. Passing a value such as `https://example.com/article?id=1` will not match the parent origin `https://example.com`, so the resize message is rejected and the iframe remains at its default height. Parse the referer and pass only its scheme/host/port origin.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Controller spec asserts a retrieval path the controller no longer implements

The test expects `TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve`, but `EmbedController#best` actually calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` when no embed exists. This expectation will fail rather than testing the implemented asynchronous behavior. The spec should assert the enqueued job and its arguments (and separately test `Jobs::RetrieveTopic` invokes `TopicRetriever`), otherwise the added test suite cannot pass and does not protect the actual contract.

Imported feed and remote HTML bypasses all post sanitization

`TopicEmbed.import` creates posts with `cook_method: raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns that raw value unchanged. RSS `i.content` and readability output are external, attacker-controlled HTML, and the embed view later renders `raw post.cooked`. A malicious or compromised feed/article can therefore persist script/event-handler markup in a topic and execute it for forum and embedded-page visitors. Imported content must be sanitized with the same allowlist/sanitizer used for posts before it is stored or rendered; merely bypassing the cooking pipeline is unsafe.

Remote importer follows redirects to unvalidated hosts

The requested embed URL is host-checked before retrieval, but `open(url).read` follows HTTP redirects without revalidating the destination. An attacker can request a URL on the configured embeddable host that redirects to an internal service or cloud metadata endpoint, causing the server-side importer to fetch that resource (SSRF). Redirect destinations must be disabled or each redirect target must be parsed, host/IP validated, and restricted before fetching.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex layout disables the right-aligned small-action button

Making `.small-action` a flex container causes its direct child `button` to become a flex item. CSS floats do not apply to flex items, so the existing `float: right` on `.small-action button` is ignored. The button will now sit immediately after `.small-action-desc` rather than at the right edge, and long descriptions can leave it incorrectly positioned or squeezed. Add flex positioning such as `margin-left: auto` to the button (and appropriate sizing for the description) instead of relying on its float.

Header panel loses its right alignment in legacy flexbox implementations

The prior `float: right` was removed and replaced with `margin-left: auto` on a flex item. The legacy flexbox implementations targeted by the new `-ms-flexbox`/`-webkit-box` declarations, notably IE10's 2012 flexbox implementation, do not reliably support auto main-axis margins. In those browsers the panel will follow the title instead of being pushed to the right, potentially causing the header controls to overlap or overflow. Provide an old-flexbox-compatible alignment fallback (for example legacy box packing/flex sizing) or retain a non-flex fallback for these browsers.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`website_name` bypasses the anonymous TL0 profile-field restriction

The new `website_name` attribute is declared as a normal serializer attribute but is not included in `untrusted_attributes`. For an anonymous viewer of a TL0 user, `website` is intentionally omitted by `restrict_user_fields?`, but `website_name` is still serialized and reveals the host (and, for same-domain URLs, the path) from that hidden website field. Add `website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` (or implement an equivalent `include_website_name?` authorization check). The currently added `include_website_name` method also lacks the required trailing `?`, so it is not the serializer inclusion hook and does not prevent this disclosure.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.

Pagination creates a phantom page for exact page-size member counts

`totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which returns 2 for a group with exactly 50 members and a limit of 50 (and similarly for every exact multiple). The Next control is therefore enabled and requests offset 50, producing an empty member page. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (while retaining the zero-member special case) so the last populated page is correctly identified.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

false_positives.candidate:
Automatic groups still render a member removal control

This item view's context is an individual `member`, so `automatic` is looked up on that user rather than on the group being edited. It will normally be undefined, making `unless automatic` true even for automatic groups. As a result, admins see a removable-x control for automatic-group members; clicking it sends a request that the server rejects. Pass the group's automatic state into the item view or conditionally render the entire member list/control from the parent group context.

Members endpoint accepts an unbounded client-controlled page size

`limit` is taken directly from the request and passed to ActiveRecord without a maximum. A request such as `?limit=1000000` can force serialization of an entire large group's membership in one response; on PostgreSQL, a negative LIMIT may also mean no limit. This public endpoint should clamp the value to a positive, bounded page size before querying to prevent expensive queries, excessive memory use, and oversized responses.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback catalogs are only eagerly loaded for controller requests

The fallback locale files are loaded only through `ApplicationController#set_locale`, while the translation accelerator automatically loads only `I18n.config.locale` during a normal `I18n.t` call. The Fallbacks backend subsequently reads the default/en locale catalog directly; it does not invoke the patched top-level translator for each fallback locale. Consequently mailers, background jobs, rake tasks, model code, and any boot-time translation that run outside an ApplicationController can report a missing translation even when it exists in the configured fallback locale. Ensure fallback locales are loaded as part of the generic translation/fallback lookup path rather than relying on the controller filter.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Advanced negative offsets cause Django QuerySet slicing errors

The advanced branch deliberately passes a negative `start_offset` to a Django `QuerySet` slice, but Django does not support negative indexing/slicing for querysets and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The cursor parser accepts signed integer offsets, so an administrator can trigger this path with an `optimized_pagination=true` request containing a cursor with a negative offset, producing a 500. Negative offsets must be rejected or translated into a supported query; they cannot be used as Python-style reverse indexes on querysets.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optimized paginator cannot paginate DateTime audit-log ordering

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to the ordered field value. The audit-log endpoint selects this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so once any results are returned, cursor construction calls this method with a `datetime` and raises `TypeError` (`datetime` does not implement floor/ceil). Subsequent cursor requests would also pass the integer cursor value directly to a datetime comparison in `build_queryset`. As a result, an authorized caller using `optimized_pagination=true` receives a 500 instead of audit-log results. This paginator needs DateTimePaginator-compatible key serialization and cursor deserialization, or the endpoint must use a paginator that supports datetime keys.

Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optimized paginator cannot paginate the audit-log datetime field

`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` selects `OptimizedCursorPaginator` while ordering by `-datetime`, but this paginator's `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `item.datetime`. Django model datetimes are `datetime` objects, so even the first optimized request reaches `build_cursor` and raises `TypeError` rather than returning a page. It also lacks the datetime cursor conversion implemented by `DateTimePaginator`, so cursor-following requests would compare the datetime column to a raw integer. The optimized paginator must support datetime keys (for example, subclass/use `DateTimePaginator` behavior) before it can be used by this endpoint.

In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

false_positives.candidate:
Changing live Redis set keys to sorted sets is not rollout-compatible

Existing buffered segments are Redis Sets (`SADD`/`SSCAN`), while this change writes the identical `span-buf:s:{...}` keys with `ZADD` and the Lua script reads/merges them with sorted-set commands. During a rolling deployment, any segment created by an old worker and still within its TTL will cause `ZADD`, `ZCARD`, or `ZUNIONSTORE` to fail with Redis `WRONGTYPE`; the processing batch then fails and spans cannot be buffered. Use versioned keys or a migration/compatibility path until all old keys have expired.

Reducing redirect traversal can split deep traces into incorrect segments

The redirect-chain traversal limit was reduced from 10,000 to 1,000 with no fallback or indication that the chain was truncated. For a trace whose spans arrive in an order that creates more than 1,000 redirects, the script stops before reaching the actual segment key, writes the new span under an intermediate key, and records a redirect to that intermediate key. Those buffers can flush separately, producing incomplete/incorrect segments. Retain the prior bound or explicitly handle a truncated traversal so the span is joined to the true root.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Eligibility is checked against the outer dataset rather than the dataset being queried

`_get_event_stats` accepts `scoped_dataset`, including calls made for dashboard split queries, but passes the captured outer `dataset` to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. In the metrics-enhanced dashboard split path, an error-only query is executed against `discover` while the captured dataset remains a metrics dataset, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns false and the error result is not upsampled. Pass `scoped_dataset` to the eligibility check so the decision describes the query that will actually execute.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

false_positives.candidate:
Discover upsampling is enabled for mixed and negated event-type queries

The Discover eligibility check is a substring match for `event.type:error`, rather than establishing that the query can only return errors. Queries such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` and `!event.type:error` contain that substring but can return transactions (which do not have the error sampling weight). Those requests will be rewritten to `upsampled_count()`, producing a weighted/missing-value total instead of the requested event count. Parse or otherwise constrain the event-type condition so the rewrite only occurs when every returned event is known to be an error.

The PR accidentally adds a gitlink pinned to the base commit

This entry is a submodule/gitlink pointing at the base revision, but no corresponding `.gitmodules` configuration is included. Clones of this revision will receive an uninitialized `sentry-repo` directory and tooling may attempt to initialize an undefined submodule. Remove this unrelated repository entry unless adding a properly configured submodule is intentional.

Weighted counts are truncated to integers

`upsampled_count` wraps `sum(sample_weight)` in `toInt64`. Sampling rates are represented as floats (the added test factory explicitly converts `client_sample_rate` to `float`), and rates such as 0.3 produce non-integral inverse weights. Casting the aggregate truncates the estimate, systematically undercounting every bucket; summing multiple fractional weights can also lose a full event. Return the sum as a numeric value, or use an explicitly specified rounding policy if integer output is required.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error IDs can be paired with the wrong nodestore records

`nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a mapping keyed by node ID and can omit records that are missing. Zipping the original `error_ids` with `events.values()` assumes both identical ordering and one value per requested ID. If any requested event is absent, all later IDs can be paired with another event's title/message/timestamp, causing the AI summary to receive incorrect error context. Look up each generated node ID explicitly and retain its associated error ID instead of consuming mapping values positionally.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged table widgets discard the query result

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with hard-coded empty `columns` and an empty `tableData` object rather than `fields`, `result.data`, and `result.meta`. Consequently every flagged dashboard table is blank regardless of the query result (and no loading/error behavior from the existing table is preserved). Pass the actual result data and metadata into the new visualization before enabling this path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Browser report timestamp/age invariants are not enforced for zero values or absent fields

Both `age` and `timestamp` are optional, and the mutual-exclusion validators test `self.initial_data.get(...)`. A report containing `age: 0` and `timestamp: 0` passes because both values are falsey; a report containing neither also passes. This accepts malformed reports despite the stated requirement to support one of the two spec formats, and allows ambiguous data to enter metrics processing. Check field presence (`"age" in initial_data` / `"timestamp" in initial_data`) and add object-level validation requiring exactly one of the two fields.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is not atomic, allowing reuse under concurrent logins

Each authorization request reads and decrypts the entire backup-code array, marks its matching entry as null locally, and then writes the full array back. Two concurrent requests using the same code can both read the original array, both validate it, and both successfully create sessions before either write occurs. Concurrent requests using different codes can also overwrite each other's consumption, restoring a code that another request already used. Consume the code with an atomic conditional database update/version check (or store individually hashed backup codes with a uniqueness/used-state condition) so only one request can claim a code.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
A backup code can be used without verifying the primary credential

The new backup-code branch authenticates whenever a supplied backup code matches, but password verification above is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is non-empty (line 121), regardless of whether that TOTP value is valid. A caller can post an email, any dummy `totpCode`, and a valid backup code directly to the credentials callback and obtain a session without the password (and can similarly bypass the identity-provider checks guarded by `!credentials.totpCode`). The UI preserves the password during the normal two-step flow, but the server must enforce this invariant itself. Require a verified primary credential before accepting either TOTP or a backup code, or use a server-bound challenge indicating that the first step was completed.

The added E2E coverage does not exercise backup-code authentication or consumption

The test only checks that generated codes can be downloaded and copied; it never logs out and signs in with a backup code, checks an invalid code is rejected, or verifies that a successfully used code cannot be reused. Those are the feature's security-critical paths, including the new credentials-provider mutation logic, and the TODO explicitly acknowledges the omission. Add end-to-end or integration coverage for valid login, invalid login, single-use behavior, and backup-code-based 2FA disablement.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google Meet fallback dereferences a missing destination calendar

`mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` when an event has no destination calendar, but the condition immediately reads `.integration`. Any booking using Google Meet without a configured destination calendar will throw before the fallback to Cal Video can run (and under strict TypeScript this is also an unsafe possibly-undefined access). Guard the value with optional chaining or an explicit existence check.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Collective hosts' calendars are discarded when the primary host has none

The event starts with `destinationCalendar: null` when neither the event type nor `organizerUser` has a destination calendar. The collective-host calendars collected in `teamDestinationCalendars` are then added with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)`, which is a no-op for `null`. Consequently, a collective booking where only a non-primary host has a calendar integration creates no calendar event for that host, despite that being the scenario this change is intended to support. Initialize the array from the team calendars when there is no primary destination.

Recurring cancellation only deletes the first calendar reference for each occurrence

For each calendar reference of the original booking, the recurring cancellation loop obtains `updBooking.references.find(...)`, which always selects only the first calendar reference of each recurring occurrence. With multiple host calendar references, the additional references are never selected for deletion; the loop instead repeatedly attempts deletion of the first event, including through unrelated credentials. This leaves cancelled recurring events on secondary hosts' calendars. Match each occurrence's reference by credential ID/external calendar ID and delete it using that reference's credential.

Rescheduling deletes multi-host calendar events with the wrong credential

The credential lookup map is keyed only by integration type, so multiple credentials for the same provider overwrite one another. The subsequent deletion iterates all booking references but retrieves credentials by `bookingRef.type`, not `bookingRef.credentialId`. After this change a collective event can have multiple Google (or other same-provider) references, causing all deletion attempts to use one host's credential; secondary host events will fail to be deleted and remain at the old time. Build the lookup by credential ID and use each reference's credential ID.

The selected destination external ID is never passed to calendar creation

`createEvent` accepts `externalId` and records it in the returned reference, but calls the calendar implementation with only `credential.id`. `EventManager` invokes this once for every destination calendar, all using the same full `calEvent.destinationCalendar` array. Integrations that choose the first destination (for example Office 365, Lark, and CalDAV) will therefore create every host's event in the first host's calendar; Google also cannot distinguish two selected calendars using the same credential because it finds the first matching credential. Pass the target external ID through the calendar creation contract and have each implementation use it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The sync-mode token schema strips the expiry fields needed by consumers

`[z.string().toString()]` does not define a Zod catch-all/index signature; it evaluates to a literal property name such as `[object Object]`. Consequently, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` only retains `access_token` (and strips arbitrary response fields). In credential-sync mode, callers such as Zoom subsequently read `newTokens.expires_in` and calculate `expiry_date` from `undefined`, producing an invalid expiry and causing the credential to remain unusable or the Prisma update to fail. The schema must explicitly accept and preserve the documented expiry field(s), e.g. via `.passthrough()`/`.catchall()` and validation of supported expiry names.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Credential-sync refresh returns a different response type than several integrations expect

When sync is enabled this helper returns the raw `fetch` `Response`, while its fallback returns whatever each supplied refresh function returns. This breaks integrations whose existing refresh functions return SDK/axios objects rather than a Fetch response. For example, HubSpot casts the result to `HubspotToken` and reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken`, while Zoho Bigin and Zoho CRM read `.data`; with a Fetch response these fields are absent, so invalid credentials are persisted or token refresh fails. Normalize the sync response to the same contract expected by each caller (or make the helper parse and return a common token payload) before replacing those calls.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Credential-sync refresh returns a different response type than several integrations expect

When sync is enabled this helper returns the raw `fetch` `Response`, while its fallback returns whatever each supplied refresh function returns. This breaks integrations whose existing refresh functions return SDK/axios objects rather than a Fetch response. For example, HubSpot casts the result to `HubspotToken` and reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken`, while Zoho Bigin and Zoho CRM read `.data`; with a Fetch response these fields are absent, so invalid credentials are persisted or token refresh fails. Normalize the sync response to the same contract expected by each caller (or make the helper parse and return a common token payload) before replacing those calls.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zoho Bigin sends a credential ID as the Cal.com user ID to the sync endpoint

`refreshOAuthTokens` expects its third argument to be the credential owner's user ID and serializes it as `calcomUserId`. This call passes `credentialId`, which is the database credential primary key captured at line 53, not `credential.userId`. A self-hosted credential source will therefore look up the wrong user (or potentially another user whose ID happens to equal that credential ID), making synced Bigin refreshes fail or return the wrong account's token.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce refresh saves the new token but uses the expired token for the current request

The newly added refresh code updates the database with `accessTokenParsed.data`, but the `jsforce.Connection` created immediately afterward still receives `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url`, which are the pre-refresh values. Since this refresh is performed while constructing the service, the first operation after an expired token will authenticate with the expired access token and fail; only a later service instance can use the saved token. Construct the connection from the refreshed response values.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Outbound token-sync requests contain no authentication

The configured credential-sync endpoint is called with only a user ID and app slug; no webhook secret, authorization header, signature, or other credential is sent. If the self-hosted endpoint follows the described contract and returns tokens for these identifiers, anyone who can reach it can request tokens for arbitrary Cal.com user IDs and apps. Require an authenticated request (for example an HMAC signature or the configured shared secret in a header) and document/verify it on the receiving service.

Salesforce service references Prisma without importing it

The new token-refresh path calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file has no `@calcom/prisma` import. This is an unresolved identifier and prevents the app-store package from type-checking/building.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest blacklist can be bypassed with email casing

Configured blacklist addresses are lowercased, but submitted guest addresses are compared without normalization. An address such as `Blocked@example.com` therefore does not match a `blocked@example.com` entry and is added/invited. Normalize submitted emails (and ideally existing-attendee comparisons) consistently before blacklist and duplicate checks.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admins are incorrectly denied permission to add guests

The authorization predicate requires a user to be both a team admin and a team owner (`isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`). These are distinct roles, so a normal team admin fails this check despite the feature/UI treating team admins or owners as authorized. Use `||` (or the existing team-admin-or-owner authorization helper) so either role can manage the booking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing attendees can receive a duplicate scheduled email

The notification call receives the original requested `guests` array rather than `uniqueGuests`, even though existing addresses are filtered out before insertion. `sendAddGuestsEmails` uses that list to decide who receives `AttendeeScheduledEmail`; thus a request containing one new address and an already-attending address sends the existing attendee a new-booking confirmation instead of the guest-added notification. Pass the actual inserted guest addresses (`uniqueGuests`) to the mailer.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_positives.candidate:
Attendees are persisted before calendar synchronization can fail

The booking attendee rows are committed at lines 92-106 before `updateCalendarAttendees` is awaited. If the calendar update fails (for example due to an expired integration credential), the mutation returns an error but the guests remain in Cal.com without calendar updates or emails, leaving booking and calendar state inconsistent. Either make failure recoverable/retryable and report the persisted state, or arrange synchronization/outbox handling so the committed attendee change is eventually applied.

The endpoint accepts an unbounded number of guest addresses

`guests` has no maximum length, while processing each address creates attendee rows, updates calendar attendees, and sends notifications to all attendees and organizers. Any authorized attendee can submit a very large array directly to this mutation and use a single booking to trigger mass email/calendar work and database writes. Impose a server-side maximum consistent with the product's guest limit before performing any writes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry increments can be lost when cron executions overlap

The retry count is calculated from the value read by `findMany` and then written as `reminder.retryCount + 1`. If two cron invocations process the same unscheduled reminder concurrently, both can read (for example) zero and both write one. The failed reminder then gets more than the intended two attempts, and concurrent scheduling attempts can continue. Use a database-side atomic increment (and ideally condition it on the reminder still being unscheduled) rather than writing a stale read value.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup deletes non-SMS workflow reminders

The `retryCount > 1` arm of this `OR` is not constrained to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. This cron endpoint will therefore permanently delete any email or WhatsApp `WorkflowReminder` whose retry count exceeds one, even though this job only processes SMS reminders. Scope the retry cleanup to unscheduled SMS reminders so retry state for other delivery methods cannot cause their reminders to be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
The public `findMany` API was removed without migrating its callers

`InsightsBookingService.findMany`, which previously executed the authorized query and accepted Prisma find-many arguments, has been removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions`. This is an exported service contract change, but this PR only updates this service and its test; any existing production caller invoking `service.findMany(...)` will fail TypeScript compilation (or fail at runtime for untyped consumers). Migrate all callers to an equivalent parameterized `$queryRaw` query as part of this change, or retain a compatible `findMany` method.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook helper cannot update .env on GNU/Linux

The command uses BSD/macOS `sed -i ''` syntax. On GNU sed, commonly used in Linux development and CI environments, `''` is treated as an input filename and the command fails rather than updating `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL`. Use a portable replacement strategy or select the `sed -i` arguments based on the platform.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not refresh the cache-status query

On successful `deleteCache`, this mutation only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation below, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, which is the query supplying `cacheUpdatedAt`; `onSuccess` is optional and is not a substitute for cache invalidation. Consequently the deleted cache continues to be displayed as present (and the delete action remains available) until an unrelated refetch/reload, especially because the query disables window-focus refetching.

Expired cache rows are reported as active cache

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups every CalendarCache row for a credential without filtering `expiresAt`. Cache reads only use rows whose `expiresAt` is in the future, so once all rows for a credential have expired this API still returns an `updatedAt` value and the UI presents it as a current cache status and offers deletion. Filter the status query to unexpired rows (consistent with `getCachedAvailability`) so the displayed status reflects cache that can actually be served.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation state updates are fired without awaiting them

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async, but this loop does not collect or await their promises. The request can proceed to completion (and, in a serverless runtime, be torn down) before the email reminder's `cancelled` flag is persisted. If that update is lost or delayed, the cron will not cancel the SendGrid send and the cancelled booking can still receive a reminder. Await these operations, e.g. with `Promise.all`, before returning.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rescheduling still creates unbounded pending SendGrid cancellations

The reschedule path passes `immediateDelete: true`, which POSTs a SendGrid `status: cancel` request and then returns without marking or deleting the local `WorkflowReminder`. The old booking remains in the database, so the cron never sees `cancelled: true` and cannot manage this record. Each reschedule therefore leaves a cancelled SendGrid scheduled-send entry until its delivery date, recreating the pending-cancellation accumulation and 100-cancellation-limit failure this PR is intended to fix; it also leaves stale workflow-reminder rows locally.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
The SendGrid client used for cancellations is never authenticated

This route calls `sgMail.setApiKey`, but the new cancellation logic uses the separate `@sendgrid/client` instance at line 57. Unlike `@sendgrid/mail`, that client is never given `SENDGRID_API_KEY` via `client.setApiKey`. Consequently the POST to `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` will be rejected as unauthorized, the catch block only logs the failure, and cancelled email reminders remain scheduled and are sent.

The one-hour cancellation window can miss reminders cancelled shortly before delivery

The cron only attempts a SendGrid cancellation for reminders whose scheduled date is within one hour, but it runs every 15 minutes. For example, after a run at 10:00 has processed the next hour, a booking cancelled at 10:01 with a reminder due at 10:05 is not processed until 10:15, after SendGrid has already delivered it. The implementation needs to cancel at cancellation time or maintain a safety margin greater than the cron interval so a cancelled booking cannot send a reminder before the next cron pass.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reschedule cancellation does not await calendar/video deletions

Using `forEach(async ...)` discards every callback promise. Before this change, `getCalendar()` was synchronous, so `deleteEvent()` was invoked before the callback returned; now the callback suspends on the dynamic import and the mutation proceeds to send email/webhooks and return without waiting for (or handling errors from) any external deletion. The booking is already marked CANCELLED, so a request-reschedule can leave the old calendar/video meeting active and any import/deletion failure becomes an unhandled rejection. Build an array of deletion promises and `await Promise.all` (with explicit error handling).

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Vital reschedules fire-and-forget external resource deletion

The async callback passed to `forEach` is not awaited by the surrounding `try/catch`. Since `getCalendar` now awaits a dynamic import, this function can finish and send the reschedule email before it has even called `deleteEvent`; failures after the await also bypass the catch block. The booking has already been cancelled at this point, so external Vital calendar/video events can remain active. Collect the callback promises and await them, preferably with per-integration error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Recurring cancellation omits dynamically imported calendar deletions from awaited work

The recurring-event path starts an `async forEach` over calendar credentials, but does not await its callbacks. Each callback now waits for `getCalendar` before pushing deletion promises into `apiDeletes`; the handler subsequently reaches `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` while `apiDeletes` is still empty or incomplete. As a result, the cancellation response and database cleanup can complete before recurring external events are deleted, and import/delete failures are unhandled. Replace the `forEach` with awaited promise collection (or an awaited loop) and add the resulting deletion promises before the final `Promise.all`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours validation ignores the booking end time

`end` is calculated from `slotStartTime` exactly like `start`, rather than from `slotEndTime`. Therefore any slot that starts before a fixed/loose host's working-hours end passes this check even if the event extends beyond that host's availability. This can make round-robin slots bookable when a required fixed host cannot attend the full event.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-day date overrides are never recognized as equal start/end times

This compares two separately-created Dayjs objects with `===`, which is always false even when `date.start` and `date.end` represent the same instant. Consequently an all-day/unavailable override skips the intended special case and can leave a slot beginning exactly at the override timestamp available (typically the first slot at midnight). Use a value comparison such as `isSame` or compare timestamps.

false_positives.candidate:
Fixed-host override checks allow slots that extend outside the override window

The override predicate only rejects a slot when its end is at/before the override start or its start is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override and ends inside it, or starts inside it and ends after it, matches neither condition and is treated as available. For a round-robin event this can expose a slot whose fixed host is unavailable for part of the booking duration; the check needs to require the entire [slot start, slot end] interval to be contained in an override range.

Multiple date-override ranges on one day are treated as an intersection

`dateOverrides.find` returns an unavailable result as soon as any same-day override does not contain the slot. With two valid availability windows on a day (for example 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-15:00), a slot inside the first window is rejected by the second window, and vice versa. Date overrides represent alternative available ranges, so a fixed host should be available when the slot is contained in any matching override, not every override.

The added regression test does not cover the fixed-host round-robin behavior being changed

The new timezone assertion uses a personal event with `hosts: []`, so it never executes the fixed-host filtering path added in `checkIfIsAvailable`. There is no test with a ROUND_ROBIN event, at least one `isFixed: true` host, and that host's date override; regressions that again expose unavailable fixed-host slots would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing integrations without webhook sender metadata cause a server error

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every active existing GitHub integration has a sender object. Integrations created through the previous setup flow did not populate this metadata (and the normal setup test's expected metadata has no `sender`), so if such an integration has no OrganizationIntegration—for example after uninstalling and attempting to install it into another organization—this raises `KeyError` and returns a 500 instead of the installation failure response. Handle missing or malformed legacy metadata explicitly, ideally by rejecting it safely or obtaining a verified sender.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
New installations can bypass the GitHub-user verification when the webhook record is not present

When no `Integration` row exists yet, this returns `pipeline.next_step()` before checking `github_authenticated_user` against an installer identity. The identity used by the later check is populated asynchronously from the GitHub installation webhook, so a user can complete the setup callback before that webhook has created the row (or when webhook delivery failed) and link an arbitrary known installation ID to their Sentry organization. This is precisely the path where the proposed authorization check is unavailable; the flow should wait for/require a verified installation sender record rather than treating a missing record as safe.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued` is evaluated once at module import rather than per assignment source

`timezone.now()` is called while the dataclass is defined, so every `AssignmentSource` created by this worker process receives the same `queued` timestamp. Consequently `to_dict()` emits a startup-time value rather than the time the webhook assignment was queued, making the context metadata incorrect and unusable for ordering, expiration, or debugging. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance gets its own timestamp.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Registered metric alert handler is now uninstantiable

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` but implements none of its abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). Because `MetricAlertFire` registers this class as its `detector_handler`, accessing `detector.detector_handler` for a metric-alert detector will raise `TypeError` instead of returning a handler, causing detector processing to fail. Keep this handler on the non-stateful base until it is implemented, or provide all required implementations.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Evaluate documentation still describes the old list return type

`StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` now returns a dictionary keyed by group key, but its docstring says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". This is the public extension point for detector implementations, so the stale documentation can cause new handlers to implement or consume the previous contract incorrectly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung spawned flusher processes are not killed before replacement

The workers are always created from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, producing `SpawnProcess` instances. On Linux, `multiprocessing.Process` refers to the default fork-context process class, so a `SpawnProcess` is not an instance of it. Consequently, when a worker is declared hung, this guard skips `process.kill()` and immediately starts a replacement. The old hung worker can remain alive and continue using Redis/Kafka concurrently with its replacement, leaking workers and potentially causing duplicate or competing flushes. The same incorrect type test at line 346 also prevents forcibly terminating a still-running spawned worker during `join`. Check against the multiprocessing base-process type or invoke `kill`/`terminate` based on capability instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Negative flusher process counts crash initialization

`--flusher-processes` accepts any integer, but a negative value is passed through as `max_processes`. `min(negative_value, shard_count)` makes `num_processes` negative, creates an empty process map, and then the shard-distribution loop indexes `self.process_to_shards_map[process_index]`, raising `KeyError` for the first assigned shard. Zero is also silently converted to the default by `max_processes or ...`, rather than being rejected or honored. Validate this CLI option as a positive integer (and validate programmatic construction similarly) before computing the process map.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Graceful shutdown stops workers before queued work is drained

`shutdown` sets every worker's `shutdown` flag before attempting to shut down the queue. A worker finishes at most the item it is currently processing and then exits its `while not self.shutdown` loop, leaving all remaining queued items unprocessed. Normal consumer shutdown/rebalance therefore abandons queued work rather than draining it, causing replayed side effects on restart and preventing a graceful shutdown from completing its in-flight workload.

Queues are unbounded, so the consumer has no backpressure

Each worker queue is created as an unbounded `queue.Queue()`, while `submit` immediately returns after enqueueing. A slow group/worker can therefore accumulate every subsequently polled Kafka message in memory; increasing the configured worker count only changes the number of unbounded queues. Under sustained input or a stuck downstream dependency this can exhaust process memory rather than applying backpressure to Kafka, contrary to the strategy's stated behavior.

Shutdown relies on Python 3.13-only queue APIs

`Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were introduced in Python 3.13. On Python 3.12 and earlier, `q.shutdown(...)` raises `AttributeError` (which is only logged), blocked worker threads remain stuck in `get()`, and the configured joins time out. The implementation must use a compatible sentinel/wakeup mechanism or raise the project's minimum Python version before using these APIs.

Worker exceptions are acknowledged as successfully processed

The worker catches every exception from `result_processor` and then unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. The commit loop can consequently commit the failed message and all later contiguous messages, permanently dropping a result after a transient database, network, or application failure. This also contradicts the strategy's documented guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing; failures need to remain outstanding or be handled through an explicit retry/DLQ policy.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache keys are ambiguous for valid resource and folder UIDs

The key concatenates `action`, `name`, and `parent` using `_` without escaping or length-prefixing the variable fields. Dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so a denial for `(name="a_b", parent="c")` produces the same key as `(name="a", parent="b_c")` for the same user/action/namespace. Once the first request is denied, the second request is returned as denied directly from the cache for 30 seconds even if its database permissions allow it. Use an unambiguous encoding of the individual fields (and preferably a distinct denial-cache key prefix).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-resource denial entries allow unbounded cache growth from request input

Every denied `Check` inserts a distinct cache entry keyed by the caller-supplied resource name and parent folder. Unlike the permission cache, whose cardinality is bounded roughly by users and actions, this cache can be populated with arbitrary nonexistent names by repeatedly issuing authorization checks. The configured TTL only bounds retention to 30 seconds and the local cache configuration has no capacity limit here, so sufficient request volume can create a large transient memory footprint (and equivalent key churn in a shared cache). Bound this cache by size/admission policy, avoid caching arbitrary nonexistent resource names, or otherwise rate-limit/normalize these entries.

Silence action is displayed but cannot open a drawer for Prometheus-only list items

Delete is hidden for Grafana rules in the ruler-free list view

canDelete now includes permissions derived from promRule, but Delete is still rendered only when rulerRule is present. GrafanaRuleListItem passes only a Prometheus rule, therefore authorized users cannot delete any Grafana-managed rule from the new alert list even though the delete modal already receives a usable identifier and group identifier.

Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
